rv.q: As a play, it is slow burning, inconsistently funny and unresolved, but it is also strange and haunting.
In fact the four scenes across two acts each has a totally different mood, ending up with extremely silly farce (with an edge to it) – and yet they all cohere into one play.
The twists and turns are pleasing, and the humour proves that, after 65 years of premieres at this venue, Ayckbourn’s still got it.

cn.t: Ayckbourn's 90th play earns praise as an astute, pensive comedy with pleasing twists that skillfully shifts moods across its scenes while offering sharp reflections on how theatre and industry have changed over decades.
